claim: Telocytes are characterized in vivo by their long projections that contact other cell types.
source: Telocytes (TCs) or interstitial cells are characterised in vivo by their long projections that contact other cell types.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of telocytes.

claim: Telocytes can be found in many different tissues including the heart, lung, and intestine.
source: Although telocytes can be found in many different tissues including the heart, lung, and intestine, their tissue-specific roles are poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about telocyte distribution.

claim: The tissue-specific roles of telocytes are poorly understood.
source: Although telocytes can be found in many different tissues including the heart, lung, and intestine, their tissue-specific roles are poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Telocytes are quiescent in homeostasis.
source: We show that telocytes are quiescent in homeostasis; however, they proliferate and serve as a major source of HGF in periodontitis.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and supported by lineage tracing data in the manuscript.

claim: Telocytes proliferate in periodontitis.
source: We show that telocytes are quiescent in homeostasis; however, they proliferate and serve as a major source of HGF in periodontitis.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and supported by lineage tracing and Ki67 staining data.

claim: Telocytes serve as a major source of HGF in periodontitis.
source: We show that telocytes are quiescent in homeostasis; however, they proliferate and serve as a major source of HGF in periodontitis.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and supported by immunostaining and scRNA-seq data.

claim: Macrophages receive telocyte-derived HGF signals and shift from an M1 to an M1/M2 state.
source: Macrophages receive telocyte-derived HGF signals and shift from an M1 to an M1/M2 state.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and supported by scRNA-seq, immunostaining, and in vitro co-culture experiments.

claim: Periodontitis is an inflammatory disease of the periodontal ligament (PDL).
source: Periodontitis is an inflammatory disease of the periodontal ligament (PDL), the tissue that connects teeth to alveolar bone.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The periodontal ligament is the tissue that connects teeth to alveolar bone.
source: Periodontitis is an inflammatory disease of the periodontal ligament (PDL), the tissue that connects teeth to alveolar bone.
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Periodontitis is a prevalent, incurable, and continuous degenerative disease that results in bone loss and tooth loss.
source: It is a prevalent, incurable, and continuous degenerative disease that results in bone loss and tooth loss.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about periodontitis characteristics.

claim: Individuals with periodontitis often exhibit gingiva recession, bleeding, and tooth mobility.
source: Individuals with periodontitis often exhibit gingiva recession, bleeding, and tooth mobility (Dentino et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: All periodontitis (with attachment loss) develops from gingivitis (no attachment loss) with poor prognosis.
source: All periodontitis (with attachment loss) develops from gingivitis (no attachment loss) with poor prognosis but not all gingivitis develops into periodontitis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about disease progression.

claim: Not all gingivitis develops into periodontitis.
source: All periodontitis (with attachment loss) develops from gingivitis (no attachment loss) with poor prognosis but not all gingivitis develops into periodontitis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about disease progression.

claim: Pathogens accumulate on the tooth surface forming plaque.
source: Briefly, pathogens accumulate on the tooth surface (forming plaque), invade the periodontium tissue, and release lipopolysaccharide (LPS), which results in inflammation and immunological events.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about periodontitis etiology.

claim: Pathogens invade the periodontium tissue and release lipopolysaccharide (LPS).
source: Briefly, pathogens accumulate on the tooth surface (forming plaque), invade the periodontium tissue, and release lipopolysaccharide (LPS), which results in inflammation and immunological events.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about periodontitis pathogenesis.

claim: LPS results in inflammation and immunological events.
source: Briefly, pathogens accumulate on the tooth surface (forming plaque), invade the periodontium tissue, and release lipopolysaccharide (LPS), which results in inflammation and immunological events.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about LPS effects.

claim: LPS causes the polarisation of pro-inflammatory macrophages (M1).
source: LPS causes the polarisation of pro-inflammatory macrophages (M1).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about macrophage polarization.

claim: M1 macrophages release cytokines such as TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-6, and IL-12.
source: M1 macrophages release cytokines such as TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-6, and IL-12, which contribute to the development and progression of inflammation-induced tissue destruction (Zhou et al., 2019a; Huang et al., 2018; Viniegra et al., 2018; de Vries et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: M1 macrophage cytokines contribute to the development and progression of inflammation-induced tissue destruction.
source: M1 macrophages release cytokines such as TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-6, and IL-12, which contribute to the development and progression of inflammation-induced tissue destruction (Zhou et al., 2019a; Huang et al., 2018; Viniegra et al., 2018; de Vries et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Understanding the regulation of the inflammatory response is critical to understanding and treating periodontitis.
source: Hence, understanding the regulation of the inflammatory response is critical to understanding and treating periodontitis.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference from the previous statements about inflammation in periodontitis.

claim: The PDL contains several different cell types.
source: The PDL, albeit only present as a thin layer, contains several different cell types.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PDL composition.

claim: The understanding of cell populations in the PDL, their interactions, signalling pathways, and how these are impacted by disease and inflammation are poorly understood.
source: However, the understanding of cell populations in the PDL, their interactions, signalling pathways, and how these are impacted by disease and inflammation are poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Telocytes have not been previously identified in the PDL.
source: In this study, we describe a cell type not previously identified in the PDL, namely, telocytes (interstitial cells).
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding of the study.

claim: Telocytes are best characterised by their unusual morphology having very long projections that make direct contacts with other cells.
source: Telocytes are an enigmatic interstitial cell type that are best characterised by their unusual morphology having very long projections that make direct contacts with other cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about telocyte characteristics.

claim: Telocytes are believed to play a role in direct cell–cell communication establishing three-dimensional networks guiding tissue organisation, mechanical sensing, regulating immune responses, and phagocytic-like properties.
source: They are believed to play a role in direct cell–cell communication establishing three-dimensional networks guiding tissue organisation, mechanical sensing, regulating immune responses, and phagocytic-like properties (Cretoiu et al., 2017; Kondo and Kaestner, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) of telocytes shows extracellular vesicles bulging out from their membranes.
source: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) of telocytes shows extracellular vesicles bulging out from their membranes, suggesting active physical communication with other cells (Cretoiu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Extracellular vesicles bulging from telocyte membranes suggest active physical communication with other cells.
source: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) of telocytes shows extracellular vesicles bulging out from their membranes, suggesting active physical communication with other cells (Cretoiu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from TEM observations, supported by citation.

claim: Possible cell signalling roles played by telocytes have not been fully described.
source: To date, possible cell signalling roles played by telocytes have not been fully described.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: In the intestine subepithelial telocytes are identified as an important source of Wnt signals to maintain the proliferation of intestinal stem cells.
source: It is only known that in the intestine subepithelial telocytes are identified as an important source of Wnt signals to maintain the proliferation of intestinal stem cells (Shoshkes-Carmel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Telocytes are identified in tissues by dual immunolabeling, most commonly CD34+/CD31-, CD34+/c-Kit+, CD34+/Vim+, and CD34+/PDGFRα+.
source: Telocytes are identified in tissues by dual immunolabeling, most commonly CD34+/CD31-, CD34+/c-Kit+, CD34+/Vim+, and CD34+/PDGFRα+ (Kondo and Kaestner, 2019; San Martin et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2020; Manetti et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: CD34+/CD31- is used to identify PDL-resident telocytes in this study.
source: In this study, we use CD34+/CD31- to identify PDL-resident telocytes combined with genetic lineage tracing and Sc-RNA sequencing to determine the role of telocytes in homeostasis and periodontitis.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Quiescent telocytes located near blood vessels are activated in periodontitis.
source: We show that quiescent telocytes located near blood vessels are activated in periodontitis and regulate macrophages via the hepatocyte growth factor (HGF)/Met signalling pathway.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study supported by lineage tracing and immunostaining data.

claim: Telocytes regulate macrophages via the hepatocyte growth factor (HGF)/Met signalling pathway.
source: We show that quiescent telocytes located near blood vessels are activated in periodontitis and regulate macrophages via the hepatocyte growth factor (HGF)/Met signalling pathway.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study supported by scRNA-seq, immunostaining, and inhibitor experiments.

claim: The transition of macrophages from an M1 to M2 state provides a possible therapeutic strategy for treating periodontitis.
source: The resulting transition of macrophages from an M1 to M2 state provides a possible therapeutic strategy for treating periodontitis.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative conclusion based on the study findings.

claim: The PDL is made up of both neural crest-derived and mesodermal-derived cell types.
source: The PDL is made up of both neural crest-derived and mesodermal-derived cell types, and we have previously described the constituent cell populations using single-cell transcriptomics (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: Adult PDL in homeostasis was compared with PDL tissue from a ligature-induced periodontitis mouse model.
source: This analysis compared adult PDL in homeostasis with PDL tissue from a ligature-induced periodontitis mouse model (Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach used in the study.

claim: 2270 cells were identified for analysis after filtering.
source: The two datasets were integrated by performing a canonical correlation analysis (CCA) (Zhao et al., 2014) identifying 2270 cells for analysis after filtering.
evidence: This is stated as a data analysis result.

claim: Cells were divided into 18 unsupervised clusters for annotation.
source: These cells were further divided into 18 unsupervised clusters for annotation (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated as a data analysis result and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: A small population of cells (cluster 14) in the mesenchymal cell population expresses Cd34 but not Cd31, and were identified as telocytes.
source: A small population of cells (cluster 14) were found in the mesenchymal cell population that expresses Cd34; however, they did not express the endothelial cell marker Cd31, and we thus identified these cells as telocytes (TCs) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from scRNA-seq analysis and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: In vitro cell culture with CD1 PDL cells at passage 1 shows characteristic telocyte structure, including podoms and podomers.
source: In vitro cell culture with CD1 PDL cells at passage 1 shows characteristic telocyte structure, including podoms (red arrows, the dilated portion) and podomers (between two arrows, the thin segments between podoms).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1c and shown in the image.

claim: Wnt1 lineage-traced cells cultured and stained with CD34 show piriform cell body and moniliform podoms and podomers.
source: Wnt1 lineage-traced cells (GFP in green) were cultured and stained with CD34 in red, which show piriform cell body and moniliform podoms (red arrows) and podomers.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1d and shown in the image.

claim: Telocytes (CD34+CD31-) were detected near blood vessels (CD34+CD31+) in vivo.
source: Telocytes (CD34+CD31-) was detected near blood vessel (CD34+CD31+) in vivo, CD34 in green, CD31 in red.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1e and shown in the image.

claim: Typical telocyte cell morphology was observed with small cell bodies and a long cellular process called telopodes.
source: Typical telocyte cell morphology was observed with small cell bodies and a long cellular process called telopodes (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from in vitro culture and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Telopodes consist of dilated portions (podoms) and thin segments in between (podomers).
source: Telopodes consist of dilated portions (podoms) and thin segments in between (podomers).
evidence: This is stated as a description of telocyte morphology.

claim: GFP-positive cells from Wnt1Cre/+;Rosa26mTmG/+ mice showed telocyte structures with podoms and podomers, which were also positive for CD34.
source: GFP-positive cells showed telocyte structures with podoms and podomers, which were also positive for CD34 (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from lineage tracing experiments and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Telocytes (CD34+/CD31-) were found in close association with blood vessels (CD34+/CD31+), had small cell nuclei, and long cell protrusions.
source: As shown in Figure 1e, telocytes (CD34+/CD31-) were found in close association with blood vessels (CD34+/CD31+), had small cell nuclei, and long cell protrusions.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunostaining and shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Pericyte markers Cd146 and Ng2 were not expressed in telocytes.
source: Therefore, to discriminate between telocytes and pericytes, we compared genes that are expressed in pericytes, Cd146 and Ng2. We found that these genes were not expressed in telocytes (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from scRNA-seq analysis and shown in Figure 1f.

claim: CD34+/CD31- telocytes are present in the PDL located in the vicinity of blood vessels.
source: These data collectively suggest that CD34+/CD31- telocytes are present in the PDL located in the vicinity of blood vessels.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from multiple lines of evidence including immunostaining and scRNA-seq.

claim: Lineage tracing using Cd34creERT2/+;Rosa26tdTomato/+ mice followed by a 1 day–1 year post-tamoxifen chase period revealed that CD34+/CD31- cell numbers did not increase to any significant extent.
source: Lineage tracing using Cd34creERT2/+;Rosa26tdTomato/+ mice (Jiang et al., 2021) followed by a 1 day–1 year post-tamoxifen chase period revealed that CD34+/CD31- cell numbers did not increase to any significant extent (Figure 2), suggesting that telocytes are a small, quiescent cell population in homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from lineage tracing experiments and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Telocytes are a small, quiescent cell population in homeostasis.
source: Lineage tracing using Cd34creERT2/+;Rosa26tdTomato/+ mice (Jiang et al., 2021) followed by a 1 day–1 year post-tamoxifen chase period revealed that CD34+/CD31- cell numbers did not increase to any significant extent (Figure 2), suggesting that telocytes are a small, quiescent cell population in homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Bone loss reached a maximum between days 4 and 7 for all three molars in the ligature-induced periodontitis model.
source: By measuring the distance between alveolar bone crest and cemento-enamel junction (ABC-CEJ distance) (Figure 3a), we found that bone loss reached a maximum between days 4 and 7 for all three molars (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from micro CT analysis and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Even though only the second molar was subjected to a ligature, the first and third molars also showed some bone loss at early time points.
source: Notably, even though only the second molar was subjected to a ligature, the first and third molars also showed some bone loss at early time points, suggesting that they are affected by the ligature-induced periodontitis to some extent.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from micro CT analysis.

claim: The first and third molar bone loss was recovered at longer time points.
source: However, the first and third molar bone loss was recovered at longer time points (Figure 3b), indicating the self-recovery ability from milder periodontitis.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from micro CT analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The recovery of bone loss in first and third molars indicates self-recovery ability from milder periodontitis.
source: However, the first and third molar bone loss was recovered at longer time points (Figure 3b), indicating the self-recovery ability from milder periodontitis.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observation of bone loss recovery.

claim: After 2 hr of ligature-induced periodontitis, there was an obvious increase in the number of CD34+/CD31- telocytes close to blood vessels.
source: After 2 hr, there was an obvious increase in the number of CD34+/CD31- telocytes close to blood vessels (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunostaining shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Cd34creERT2/+;Rosa26tdTomato/+ mice tracing for 7 days showed an increase in tdTomato+/CD31- cells in periodontitis.
source: Cd34creERT2/+;Rosa26tdTomato/+ mice (Jiang et al., 2021) tracing for 7 days also showed an increase in tdTomato+/CD31- cells in periodontitis (Figure 3d and e, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from lineage tracing experiments shown in Figures 3d and 3e.

claim: Telocytes expressed the proliferation marker Ki67 in periodontitis.
source: These telocytes also expressed the proliferation marker Ki67 (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunostaining shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Telocytes proliferate in the PDL following ligature-induced periodontitis.
source: These data indicate that telocytes proliferate in the PDL following ligature-induced periodontitis.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from lineage tracing and Ki67 staining data.

claim: Telocytes can secrete extracellular vesicles.
source: It has been demonstrated that telocytes can secrete extracellular vesicles (Cretoiu et al., 2016), suggesting that they may have a role in cell signalling.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Telocytes may have a role in cell signalling.
source: It has been demonstrated that telocytes can secrete extracellular vesicles (Cretoiu et al., 2016), suggesting that they may have a role in cell signalling.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observation that telocytes secrete extracellular vesicles.

claim: Gene enrichment analysis identified angiogenesis, leukocyte migration and inflammatory responses as the three top pathways in PDL telocytes.
source: Gene enrichment analysis of the single-cell RNA-seq datasets identified angiogenesis, leukocyte migration and inflammatory responses as the three top pathways in PDL telocytes (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from gene enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The CHEMERIN, HGF, IFN-I, IL16, LIFR, and APELIN pathways are not active during homeostasis but are active in periodontitis.
source: We identified the CHEMERIN, HGF, IFN-I, IL16, LIFR, and APELIN pathways as not being active during homeostasis but rather, to be active in periodontitis (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from cell-cell communication analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Telocytes were found to express Hgf and Flt3.
source: Telocytes were found to express Hgf and Flt3 (Figure 4b), highlighting a potential role for the HGF signalling pathway.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: HGF was originally found in liver as a potential hepatocyte mitogen.
source: HGF was originally found in liver as a potential hepatocyte mitogen (Nakamura et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: HGF is involved in repair and regeneration as a healing factor.
source: It is involved in repair and regeneration as a healing factor (Matsumoto et al., 2014; Ko et al., 2018; Yang and Ming, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: RNA-seq cell–cell communication analysis identified macrophages as a target of HGF signalling from telocytes in mouse ligature-induced periodontitis.
source: In mouse ligature-induced periodontitis, our RNA-seq cell–cell communication analysis identified macrophages as a target of HGF signalling from telocytes (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from cell-cell communication analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Telocytes are identified as potentially interacting with macrophage clusters 1 and 4.
source: Of the four macrophage clusters identified, telocytes are identified as potentially interacting with macrophage clusters 1 and 4.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: Endothelial cells (CD34+/CD31+) did not express HGF.
source: Endothelial cells (CD34+/CD31+) did not express HGF, whereas telocytes (CD34+/CD31-) with telopodes expressed HGF (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunostaining shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Telocytes (CD34+/CD31-) with telopodes expressed HGF.
source: Endothelial cells (CD34+/CD31+) did not express HGF, whereas telocytes (CD34+/CD31-) with telopodes expressed HGF (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunostaining shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Telocytes are the only cells that produce HGF in periodontitis based on ScRNA-seq analysis.
source: In conclusion, telocytes express HGF and, based on the ScRNA-seq analysis, are the only cells that produce this signal in periodontitis.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from scRNA-seq and immunostaining data.

claim: Macrophages express the HGF receptor (HGFR), encoded by Met.
source: The recipient cells are macrophages which express the HGF receptor (HGFR), encoded by Met (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Four clusters of macrophages were identified from the single-cell transcriptomics analysis.
source: Four clusters of macrophages were identified from the single-cell transcriptomics analysis (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Macrophage cluster 1 expresses Acod1 and Trem1.
source: Differentially expressed gene (DEG) analysis suggested macrophage cluster 1 express Acod1, Trem1; macrophage cluster 2 express Mc4a4c, Ccr2; macrophage cluster 3 express Aif1, Mrc1; macrophage cluster 4 express Cd36, Arg1 (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from DEG analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Macrophage cluster 2 expresses Mc4a4c and Ccr2.
source: Differentially expressed gene (DEG) analysis suggested macrophage cluster 1 express Acod1, Trem1; macrophage cluster 2 express Mc4a4c, Ccr2; macrophage cluster 3 express Aif1, Mrc1; macrophage cluster 4 express Cd36, Arg1 (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from DEG analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Macrophage cluster 3 expresses Aif1 and Mrc1.
source: Differentially expressed gene (DEG) analysis suggested macrophage cluster 1 express Acod1, Trem1; macrophage cluster 2 express Mc4a4c, Ccr2; macrophage cluster 3 express Aif1, Mrc1; macrophage cluster 4 express Cd36, Arg1 (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from DEG analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Macrophage cluster 4 expresses Cd36 and Arg1.
source: Differentially expressed gene (DEG) analysis suggested macrophage cluster 1 express Acod1, Trem1; macrophage cluster 2 express Mc4a4c, Ccr2; macrophage cluster 3 express Aif1, Mrc1; macrophage cluster 4 express Cd36, Arg1 (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from DEG analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: In re-clustered macrophages, clusters on the left are cells from periodontitis and right from homeostasis.
source: In each re-clustered plot, clusters on the left are cells from periodontitis and right from homeostasis – they are clearly separated and the periodontitis cells occur in three linked clusters (0, 3, and 6) (Figure 5b, e, and f).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from re-clustering analysis shown in Figures 5b, e, and f.

claim: Periodontitis macrophage cells occur in three linked clusters (0, 3, and 6).
source: In each re-clustered plot, clusters on the left are cells from periodontitis and right from homeostasis – they are clearly separated and the periodontitis cells occur in three linked clusters (0, 3, and 6) (Figure 5b, e, and f).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from re-clustering analysis shown in Figures 5b, e, and f.

claim: The HGF signalling pathway has a sole ligand–receptor pair, HGF and HGFR (Met).
source: The HGF signalling pathway has a sole ligand–receptor pair, HGF and HGFR (Met).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the HGF signaling pathway.

claim: Macrophages expressing Met also expressed Arg1 and Nos2.
source: Interestingly, in the datasets, macrophages expressing Met also expressed Arg1 (encodes Arginase1 [Arg1]) and Nos2 (encodes inducible nitric oxide synthase [iNOS]) (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: iNOS mediates the pathological effect of LPS in periodontitis and is a marker of inflammatory M1 macrophages.
source: In periodontitis, iNOS mediates the pathological effect of LPS and it is a marker of inflammatory M1 macrophages, which are an indicator of disease progression (Italiani and Boraschi, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Arg1 is a gene expressed in M2 macrophages.
source: Arg1, a gene expressed in M2 macrophages, however, is believed to decrease LPS-induced pro-inflammatory cytokine production (Italiani and Boraschi, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Arg1 is believed to decrease LPS-induced pro-inflammatory cytokine production.
source: Arg1, a gene expressed in M2 macrophages, however, is believed to decrease LPS-induced pro-inflammatory cytokine production (Italiani and Boraschi, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Macrophages activated by HGF signals in the PDL can be considered to be in an M1/M2 state.
source: Therefore, macrophages activated by HGF signals in the PDL can be considered to be in an M1/M2 state.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observation that these macrophages express both M1 and M2 markers.

claim: Monocytes in an inflammatory environment first polarise to M1, then M2 subject to microenvironmental signals.
source: Previous studies indicate that monocytes in an inflammatory environment first polarise to M1, then M2 subject to microenvironmental signals (Yang et al., 2018; Bronte and Zanovello, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Arg1 competes with iNOS for their common substrate l-arginine.
source: It is well known that Arg1 competes with iNOS for their common substrate l-arginine (Italiani and Boraschi, 2014; Nishikoba et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HGF/Met is reported to induce Met+/Nos2+ macrophages to an M2-like phenotype via overexpression of Arg1.
source: Moreover, HGF/Met is reported to induce Met+/Nos2+ macrophages to an M2-like phenotype via overexpression of Arg1 (Nishikoba et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Macrophages in PDL do not express Met protein during homeostasis.
source: During homeostasis, macrophages in PDL do not express Met protein; however, macrophages start to express Met in periodontitis (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunostaining shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Macrophages start to express Met in periodontitis.
source: During homeostasis, macrophages in PDL do not express Met protein; however, macrophages start to express Met in periodontitis (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunostaining shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Met-expressing cells are located in close proximity to the telopodes of telocytes.
source: Met-expressing cells are located in close proximity to the telopodes of telocytes (Figure 5d), indicating that telocytes likely make physical contact with Met+ macrophages.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunostaining shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Telocytes likely make physical contact with Met+ macrophages.
source: Met-expressing cells are located in close proximity to the telopodes of telocytes (Figure 5d), indicating that telocytes likely make physical contact with Met+ macrophages.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observation of close proximity shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Telocytes promote the overexpression of Arg1 in periodontitis which leads to the M1/M2 state of macrophages.
source: Thus, it is conceivable that telocytes promote the overexpression of Arg1 in periodontitis which further leads to the M1/M2 state of macrophages.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative conclusion based on the observations.

claim: RNA velocity analysis suggests that Arg1+/Nos2+ macrophages in cluster 0 are linked with Ccr2hiAif1lo (cluster 3) cells and Ccr2loAif1hi cells (cluster 6).
source: Additionally, RNA velocity analysis suggests that these Arg1+/Nos2+ macrophages present in cluster 0 (Figure 5b) are linked with Ccr2hiAif1lo (cluster 3) cells and Ccr2loAif1hi cells (cluster 6) (Figure 5e and f).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from RNA velocity analysis shown in Figures 5e and f.

claim: When tivantinib was administered to mice with ligature-induced periodontitis, Arg1+ cell numbers significantly decreased.
source: We observed that when tivantinib was administered to mice with ligature-induced periodontitis, Arg1+ cell numbers significantly decreased (Figure 6a and b), indicating that inhibition of the HGF-Met signalling interaction in macrophages blocks their polarisation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from in vivo inhibitor experiments shown in Figures 6a and b.

claim: Inhibition of the HGF-Met signalling interaction in macrophages blocks their polarisation.
source: We observed that when tivantinib was administered to mice with ligature-induced periodontitis, Arg1+ cell numbers significantly decreased (Figure 6a and b), indicating that inhibition of the HGF-Met signalling interaction in macrophages blocks their polarisation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the tivantinib inhibitor experiments.

claim: FAC-sorted CD34+/CD31- telocytes co-cultured with M0/M1 macrophages led to a significant increase in Arg1 expression with simultaneous reduction in Inos expression compared to control macrophage-only cultures.
source: Upon analysing the expression levels of Inos and Arg1 by qPCR, in comparison to control macrophage-only cultures, the presence of telocytes led to a significant increase in Arg1 expression with simultaneous reduction in Inos expression (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from in vitro co-culture experiments shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The increase in Arg1 and reduction in Inos in macrophages co-cultured with telocytes did not occur when tivantinib was added to the culture.
source: However, this did not occur when tivantinib was added to the culture (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from in vitro co-culture experiments with inhibitor shown in Figure 6c.

claim: M1 macrophages respond to HGF signals secreted by telocytes via Met to adopt an M1/M2 phenotype.
